heat-treatment-001.question: Which statement about the martensitic transformation in steel is correct?
choices: It proceeds slowly as carbon atoms diffuse over long distances and precipitate cementite at the austenite grain boundaries
It is a diffusionless shear transformation producing body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon
The slower the cooling rate, the more time the carbon atoms have to diffuse and rearrange, so the more martensite forms in the steel
heat-treatment-001.explanation: When austenite is quenched faster than the critical cooling rate, carbon has no time to diffuse, and a shear-type transformation occurs in which atoms shift cooperatively by small amounts, producing body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon. Because the carbon distorts the lattice along the c axis, martensite is very hard and brittle. The transformation starts at the Ms temperature and progresses as the temperature falls, with almost no dependence on holding time. Pearlite and bainite are the structures that separate into ferrite and cementite with carbon diffusion, and it is pearlite that forms more readily the slower the cooling.

heat-treatment-002.question: Which correctly describes the difference between a TTT (isothermal transformation) diagram and a CCT (continuous cooling transformation) diagram?
choices: A TTT diagram shows transformation when the steel is quenched to a fixed temperature and held there, while a CCT diagram shows transformation during continuous cooling
A TTT diagram shows transformation during continuous cooling, while a CCT diagram shows transformation when the steel is held at a fixed temperature
The two contain the same information, with the vertical and horizontal axes swapped
heat-treatment-002.explanation: A TTT diagram shows the start and finish times of transformation when austenitized steel is quenched to a given temperature fast enough to avoid transformation and then held at that temperature; it is used to design isothermal treatments such as austempering. When the temperature falls continuously, as in actual quenching, the CCT diagram applies, and its transformation start line is shifted to longer times and lower temperatures than in the TTT diagram. The choice assigning continuous cooling to the TTT diagram and isothermal holding to the CCT diagram swaps the two definitions. Both are separate diagrams with temperature on the vertical axis and time (logarithmic) on the horizontal axis, and cooling faster than the nose gives martensite.

heat-treatment-003.question: Adding alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo to steel improves its hardenability. Which is the correct reason?
choices: The nose of the TTT diagram moves to shorter times, so austenite transforms faster and the steel hardens more easily
The nose of the TTT diagram moves to longer times, so martensite forms more easily even with slow cooling
The Ms temperature rises, so martensite starts to form earlier in cooling
heat-treatment-003.explanation: Hardenability is the depth to which martensite can be obtained by quenching (how readily the steel hardens). Alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo retard the pearlite and bainite transformations of austenite and move the nose of the TTT and CCT diagrams to longer times. This lowers the critical cooling rate, so martensite forms more easily at the center of thick sections or with slower cooling such as oil quenching. If the nose moved to shorter times, the steel would harden less readily. Most alloying elements actually lower the Ms temperature, so that is not the reason for improved hardenability. Hardenability is evaluated with the Jominy end-quench test.

heat-treatment-004.question: What is the main purpose of tempering a quenched steel?
choices: To make the martensite even harder and raise its wear resistance
To increase retained austenite, stabilizing the microstructure and preventing dimensional change
To restore toughness and reduce internal stresses at the cost of some hardness
heat-treatment-004.explanation: As-quenched martensite is hard but very brittle and carries large internal stresses. In tempering, the steel is reheated to a temperature below the A1 temperature (727 °C); the supersaturated carbon precipitates as fine carbides and internal stresses relax, so hardness falls but toughness recovers substantially. The higher the tempering temperature, the softer and tougher the structure; low-temperature tempering is used for tools and high-temperature tempering for machine parts (the combination with the preceding quench is called quenching and tempering). An increase in hardness on tempering is limited to secondary hardening in certain alloy steels and is not the general purpose. Tempering tends to decompose retained austenite; increasing it is not the aim.

heat-treatment-005.question: The yield stress of a steel follows the Hall–Petch relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d with σ₀ = 70 MPa and k = 0.74 MPa·√m. Which value is closest to the yield stress for an average grain size d = 25 µm?
choices: About 75 MPa
About 148 MPa
About 218 MPa
heat-treatment-005.explanation: Converting the grain size to meters gives d = 25×10⁻⁶ m and √d = 5.0×10⁻³ √m, so k/√d = 0.74/(5.0×10⁻³) = 148 MPa. Hence σy = 70 + 148 = 218 MPa. About 75 MPa results from leaving the grain size in mm as d = 0.025, so the units of k (MPa·√m) and of the grain size do not match. About 148 MPa is only the grain boundary strengthening contribution, forgetting to add σ₀. Grain refinement is one of the few strengthening methods that raises strength and toughness at the same time, and it is exploited in processes such as controlled rolling of steel. When the grain size shrinks to the nanometer scale, the relation can break down.

heat-treatment-006.question: The yield stress of a metal was 150 MPa at an average grain size of 100 µm and 250 MPa at 25 µm. Assuming the Hall–Petch relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d, which value is closest to the yield stress at a grain size of 4 µm?
choices: About 278 MPa
About 550 MPa
About 950 MPa
heat-treatment-006.explanation: Converting the grain sizes to meters and computing 1/√d gives 100 for d = 100 µm, 200 for 25 µm and 500 for 4 µm (all in 1/√m). From the two data points, k = (250 − 150)/(200 − 100) = 1.0 MPa·√m and σ₀ = 150 − 1.0 × 100 = 50 MPa, so at 4 µm, σy = 50 + 1.0 × 500 = 550 MPa. About 950 MPa is the mistake of drawing a straight line assuming the yield stress is proportional to 1/d, and about 278 MPa extrapolates as if the yield stress varied linearly with grain size d. The strengthening is inversely proportional to the square root of the grain size, so each time the grain size is reduced to 1/4, the grain boundary contribution doubles.

heat-treatment-007.question: Which is the correct sequence for precipitation hardening an Al-Cu alloy (duralumin type)?
choices: Solution treatment → quench → aging
Aging → solution treatment → slow cooling
Quench → solution treatment → annealing
heat-treatment-007.explanation: First, a solution treatment holds the alloy above the solvus to dissolve the Cu, and quenching carries the supersaturated solid solution down to room temperature. Holding it at room temperature (natural aging) or at about 100–200 °C (artificial aging) then forms fine precipitates that are coherent or semicoherent with the matrix, such as GP zones, θ″ and θ′, which obstruct dislocation motion and raise the strength. Aging for too long coarsens the stable θ phase (Al₂Cu) and lowers the strength, which is overaging. Slow cooling after solution treatment precipitates coarse equilibrium phases that do not help strengthening, so the quench is essential.

heat-treatment-008.question: Which of the following aluminum alloys cannot be strengthened by precipitation-hardening heat treatment (that is, is non-heat-treatable)?
choices: 2000 series (Al-Cu)
5000 series (Al-Mg)
6000 series (Al-Mg-Si)
heat-treatment-008.explanation: The 5000 series (Al-Mg) are non-heat-treatable alloys that get their strength from solid-solution strengthening by Mg and from work hardening by cold working. They have excellent corrosion resistance and weldability and are used for ships and tanks. The 2000 series (Al-Cu), typified by duralumin, are heat-treatable and strengthened by Al-Cu precipitates. The 6000 series (Al-Mg-Si) are also heat-treatable, using Mg-Si precipitates, and are widely used for extrusions. In addition, the 7000 series (Al-Zn-Mg) are the strongest heat-treatable alloys, while the 1000 series (pure aluminum) and 3000 series (Al-Mn) are non-heat-treatable. Learn to tell from the alloy system whether the strengthening mechanism is precipitation or work hardening.

heat-treatment-009.question: Which statement about substitutional solid-solution strengthening is correct?
choices: The larger the size difference between solute and solvent atoms, the more the lattice is disordered and the more easily dislocations move, so the smaller the strengthening effect
Increasing the solute concentration generally lowers strength and raises ductility, so alloys become softer than the pure metal
The lattice strain field around solute atoms interacts with dislocations and hinders their motion
heat-treatment-009.explanation: Solute atoms differ from the host atoms in size and elastic modulus, so they create lattice strain fields around themselves. These strain fields interact with the strain fields of dislocations and pin them, so a larger stress is needed to move dislocations. This is solid-solution strengthening, and the effect is larger the greater the atomic size difference (size effect) and the modulus difference. Within the solubility limit, increasing the solute concentration generally raises strength and slightly lowers ductility. Brass (Cu-Zn), Al-Mg alloys, and Si and Mn in steel are typical examples of solid-solution strengthening.

heat-treatment-010.question: A copper wire 10.0 mm in diameter is drawn down to 8.0 mm. What is the percent cold work (reduction in area)?
heat-treatment-010.explanation: Percent cold work is the reduction in cross-sectional area, %CW = (A₀ − A_d)/A₀ × 100. Because area is proportional to the square of the diameter, %CW = (10.0² − 8.0²)/10.0² × 100 = (100 − 64)/100 × 100 = 36%. 20% is the reduction in diameter, (10.0 − 8.0)/10.0, and 56% is the mistake of dividing by the area after drawing ((100 − 64)/64 ≈ 0.56). The greater the cold work, the higher the dislocation density and the more the metal work-hardens: strength rises but ductility falls. The amount of cold work also affects the recrystallization temperature and the grain size after recrystallization.

heat-treatment-011.question: Which statement about recrystallization when a cold-worked metal is heated is correct?
choices: New, nearly strain-free grains form; strength falls and ductility is restored
The greater the cold work, the higher the recrystallization temperature
After recrystallization ends, grains stop growing even if heating continues
heat-treatment-011.explanation: When a cold-worked metal is heated, recovery occurs first, as dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall; at higher temperatures, recrystallization follows, with new, nearly strain-free grains nucleating and growing, driven by the stored strain energy. Because the dislocation density drops greatly, strength and hardness decrease and ductility is restored. The greater the cold work, the larger the stored energy, so the recrystallization temperature is lower. A rough guide for the recrystallization temperature is 0.3–0.5 times the melting point (in absolute temperature), but it varies with the amount of cold work and the purity. If heating continues after recrystallization, grain growth proceeds to reduce the grain boundary energy.

heat-treatment-012.question: An aluminum alloy reaches peak hardness after 10 hours of aging at 190 °C. If the aging rate follows the Arrhenius form with an activation energy of 120 kJ/mol, which value is closest to the time needed to reach peak hardness at 160 °C? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 1.2 hours
About 12 hours
About 87 hours
heat-treatment-012.explanation: If the reaction rate is proportional to exp(−Q/RT), the time to reach the same state is t ∝ exp(Q/RT). With T₁ = 463 K and T₂ = 433 K, t₂ = t₁ × exp[(Q/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)] = 10 × exp(14433 × 1.495×10⁻⁴) = 10 × exp(2.16) ≈ 87 hours. About 1.2 hours reverses the sign of the exponent, giving a shorter time even though the temperature was lowered. About 12 hours assumes the time is inversely proportional to the temperature in °C. The roughly ninefold increase in time for a difference of only 30 °C reflects the strong temperature dependence of the Arrhenius form.

heat-treatment-013.question: Which statement correctly describes normalizing of steel?
choices: The steel is heated into the austenite region and then cooled in still air, giving a uniform, fine-grained ferrite and pearlite structure
The steel is heated into the austenite region and then quenched in water or oil, turning it entirely into hard martensite
The steel is heated into the austenite region and then cooled slowly in the furnace, giving the softest, most workable structure
heat-treatment-013.explanation: Normalizing heats the steel about 30–50°C above the A3 point (the Acm point for hypereutectoid steel) into the austenite region to make uniform austenite, and then cools it in still air. Coarse or nonuniform structures from forging or casting are refined into a standard fine-grained ferrite and pearlite structure. Cooling is faster than in furnace annealing, so the pearlite is finer and the strength and toughness are somewhat higher. Quenching in water or oil to form martensite is hardening. Slow cooling in the furnace to soften the steel is full annealing, done before machining or cold working.

heat-treatment-014.question: Which correctly describes what the Jominy end-quench test of steel examines?
choices: Quenched specimens are tempered at different temperatures and their hardness measured, to compare how easily they soften on tempering
An indenter is pressed into the surface of a quenched specimen, and the amount of retained austenite is found from the indentation depth
A heated round bar is cooled by spraying water on one end only, and hardenability is compared from the hardness at each distance from that end
heat-treatment-014.explanation: In the Jominy test, an austenitized round bar (about 25 mm in diameter) is cooled by a water jet sprayed from below onto one end only. The cooling rate decreases with distance from the quenched end, so measuring the hardness at each distance gives, in a single curve, the relation between cooling rate and the ease of forming martensite. In alloy steels with high hardenability, the hardness falls off little even far from the quenched end. The hardness at the quenched end is set mainly by the carbon content, while hardenability shows up as the distance at which the hardness begins to fall. Softening on tempering is studied by tests at different tempering temperatures, and the amount of retained austenite is measured by methods such as X-ray diffraction.

heat-treatment-015.question: The Ms temperature of a steel is 220°C. Assuming the volume fraction of martensite formed on quenching follows the Koistinen-Marburger equation f = 1 − exp[−0.011(Ms − T)] (temperatures in °C), which is closest to the fraction of retained austenite after quenching to 20°C?
choices: About 0%
About 11%
About 89%
heat-treatment-015.explanation: Since Ms − T = 220 − 20 = 200, the martensite fraction is f = 1 − exp(−0.011 × 200) = 1 − exp(−2.2) ≈ 1 − 0.111 = 0.889. The retained austenite is the remaining fraction, about 11%. About 89% mistakes the martensite fraction for the retained austenite. About 0% assumes that everything transforms once the steel is cooled below Ms; in fact the amount of martensite is set not by holding time but by how far below Ms the steel is cooled. More carbon or alloying lowers Ms, which increases the retained austenite at room temperature. Retained austenite can transform in service and change dimensions, so it is reduced by subzero treatment, cooling below 0°C.

heat-treatment-016.question: Which statement about the austempering of steel is correct?
choices: The steel is quenched into a salt bath just above Ms, held until inside and outside reach the same temperature, removed before transformation starts and air-cooled to martensite
The steel is quenched into a salt bath below the nose and above Ms and held there until the transformation to bainite is complete
The steel is heated above A1 and cooled slowly in the furnace to give coarse pearlite and the softest condition
heat-treatment-016.explanation: In austempering, austenitized steel is quenched into a salt bath or similar medium at a temperature below the nose of the TTT diagram and above Ms, and held there until the isothermal transformation to bainite is complete. Because no martensite forms, quench cracking and distortion are small, and the toughness can exceed that of quenched-and-tempered steel of the same hardness; it is used for springs, thin parts and austempered ductile iron. Removing the part before transformation starts and air-cooling it to martensite is martempering (marquenching). Furnace cooling to coarse pearlite is full annealing.

heat-treatment-017.question: What is the main purpose of spheroidize annealing, applied to bearing steels (high-carbon chromium steels) and tool steels before hardening?
choices: To turn lamellar or networked cementite into particles, softening the steel and making machining and cold working easier
To refine lamellar pearlite further and raise the hardness so that the steel can be used without hardening
To dissolve all the cementite in austenite and retain the austenite all the way to room temperature
heat-treatment-017.explanation: Spheroidize annealing holds steel just below A1, or around A1, for a long time, or cycles it across A1, so that the lamellar cementite of pearlite and the grain-boundary network of cementite in hypereutectoid steels change into particles (spheroids), which have less surface energy. The cementite particles are dispersed in a ferrite matrix, so the hardness falls, machinability and cold workability improve, and the structure becomes a good starting point for uniform hardening. Refining pearlite is the purpose of normalizing and does not replace hardening. Nor is spheroidizing a treatment that retains austenite at room temperature.

heat-treatment-018.question: What mainly determines the hardness of as-quenched martensite? Assume the steel was cooled fast enough to become fully martensitic.
choices: The amount of alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo; the more hardenability-raising elements, the harder it is
The cooling rate; even beyond the critical cooling rate, faster cooling gives a harder structure
The carbon content; the more supersaturated carbon in solution, the harder it is
heat-treatment-018.explanation: The hardness of martensite is set mainly by the amount of supersaturated carbon in solution. Carbon distorts the lattice and strongly obstructs dislocation motion, so the hardness rises steeply with carbon; above about 0.6-0.7% C, however, the as-quenched hardness of the steel levels off because soft retained austenite increases. Alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo raise hardenability (the depth of hardening) but have little effect on the hardness of a fully martensitic structure. Once the critical cooling rate is exceeded the structure is martensite, so cooling faster hardly changes the hardness and only increases the risk of quench cracking and distortion.

heat-treatment-019.question: The isothermal transformation of austenite to pearlite in a steel follows the Avrami equation f = 1 − exp(−ktⁿ) (f is the transformed fraction) with n = 3. If 50% transformation takes 100 s at a certain temperature, which is closest to the time for 90% transformation?
choices: About 149 s
About 180 s
About 332 s
heat-treatment-019.explanation: For f = 0.5, kt₅₀ⁿ = ln 2, and for f = 0.9, kt₉₀ⁿ = ln 10, so t₉₀/t₅₀ is (ln 10/ln 2) to the power 1/n. (2.303/0.693) = 3.32 to the power 1/3 is about 1.49, so t₉₀ ≈ 149 s. About 332 s forgets the power 1/n, and about 180 s assumes that time is proportional to the transformed fraction. In the Avrami equation nucleation and growth combine to give an S-shaped curve: slow at first, fast in the middle and slow again at the end. The start and finish curves of a TTT diagram join, at each temperature, the times for, say, 1% and 99% transformation.

heat-treatment-020.question: In induction hardening of steel, what happens to the depth of the hardened layer when the frequency of the induction current is raised?
choices: The eddy currents flow more easily to the center, so the hardened layer becomes deeper
The skin effect concentrates the current at the surface, so the hardened layer becomes shallower
The frequency changes only the heating rate and has no effect on the depth of the hardened layer
heat-treatment-020.explanation: In induction heating, the alternating magnetic field of a coil induces eddy currents in the steel, and their Joule heat does the heating. The skin effect concentrates alternating current near the surface, and the depth through which it flows (the penetration depth) is inversely proportional to the square root of the frequency, so a higher frequency concentrates the heating at the surface and gives a shallower hardened layer. High frequencies are therefore chosen for shallow cases and low frequencies for deep ones. Because only the surface is rapidly heated and quenched to martensite, the core stays tough and compressive residual stress remains at the surface, raising fatigue strength. The claim that frequency does not affect the depth is wrong.

heat-treatment-021.question: When heated steel is quenched in water or oil, the way its surface cools changes in stages. Which description is correct?
choices: A vapor blanket first insulates the surface and cooling is slow; it is fastest when the blanket collapses into boiling, then slow convection follows
Cooling is fastest right after immersion, and then the cooling rate keeps falling at a steady proportional rate as the temperature difference shrinks
Vigorous boiling at first gives the fastest cooling; as the bath temperature is approached a vapor blanket covers the surface, and cooling ends slowly through it
heat-treatment-021.explanation: When hot steel enters the quenchant, the liquid at the surface flashes to vapor and forms a vapor blanket. Vapor conducts heat poorly, so cooling in this vapor-blanket stage is surprisingly slow. As the surface cools, the blanket can no longer be sustained and collapses; liquid then touches the surface directly and boils vigorously, and the heat of vaporization gives the fastest cooling. When the temperature falls near the boiling point of the quenchant, boiling stops and slow cooling by convection follows. Statements that cooling is fastest just after immersion, or that a vapor blanket forms after boiling, do not fit this sequence. Patches of remaining vapor blanket cause soft spots, so the part or the quenchant is agitated to break the blanket early.

heat-treatment-022.question: When round bars of the same carbon steel are water-quenched under the same conditions, the larger the diameter, the lower the hardness at the center. Which correctly explains this mass effect?
choices: In thicker bars carbon segregates toward the center, so the martensite at the center holds less carbon and is softer
In thicker bars the surface cools more slowly, so the center turns to martensite before the surface and ends up softer
In thicker bars the center cools more slowly, falls short of the critical cooling rate, and forms pearlite or bainite
heat-treatment-022.explanation: In quenching, heat escapes through the surface, so the center cools more slowly than the surface, and the difference grows with diameter. If the cooling rate at the center falls below the critical cooling rate needed to miss the nose of the CCT diagram, pearlite or bainite forms instead of martensite and hardness drops. This is the mass effect. Alloy steels with Mn, Cr, Mo and similar additions for higher hardenability have lower critical cooling rates, so even thick parts harden to the center and the mass effect is smaller. Bar size does not redistribute carbon. The center never cools before the surface, so the statement that the center becomes martensite first is also wrong.

heat-treatment-023.question: After tempering, steels such as Ni–Cr steels can suffer a large drop in impact energy if they are cooled slowly through, or held for long in, the range around 500 °C (temper embrittlement). Which combination of main cause and remedy is correct?
choices: Martensite reverts to austenite in this temperature range; it is prevented by tempering above the A₁ temperature instead
Impurities such as P and Sb segregate to prior-austenite grain boundaries; it is prevented by fast cooling after tempering and adding Mo
The carbides precipitated during tempering all redissolve and the hardness returns; it is prevented by shortening the tempering time
heat-treatment-023.explanation: This temper embrittlement occurs when, after tempering, the steel passes slowly through or is held in the range around 500 °C (roughly 375–575 °C), so that impurity elements such as P, Sb and Sn gather at the grain boundaries of the austenite that existed before quenching (prior-austenite grain boundaries) and weaken the bonding there. Fracture becomes intergranular and the ductile-brittle transition temperature rises. Remedies are lowering the impurity content, cooling quickly after tempering (for example by water cooling) to pass through the range rapidly, and adding a little Mo, which suppresses the effect of segregation. Tempering below A₁ does not revert martensite to austenite, and heating above A₁ would destroy the quenched structure itself. No mechanism exists by which carbides redissolve and restore hardness.

heat-treatment-024.question: Which statement correctly relates the morphology of martensite in steel to carbon content?
choices: Whatever the carbon content, martensite always consists of thin plates stacked in parallel, with the same internal structure
Low-carbon steels form lenticular (plate) martensite and high-carbon steels lath martensite, and the higher the carbon, the tougher it is
Low-carbon steels form long thin laths and high-carbon steels lenticular (plate) martensite, which contains fine internal twins
heat-treatment-024.explanation: Steels with little carbon (roughly 0.6% or less) form lath martensite, in which long thin laths line up in parallel bundles; the inside has a high dislocation density, and toughness is relatively good. Steels with more carbon (roughly 1% or more) form lenticular (plate) martensite, in which lens-shaped plates form at angles to one another and contain fine transformation twins. It is hard but brittle, and microcracks can form where plates impinge. Intermediate carbon contents give a mixture. Statements that swap the low- and high-carbon morphologies, or that the morphology does not depend on carbon, are wrong. The fall in the Ms temperature with carbon content is also linked to this change in morphology.

heat-treatment-025.question: The Ms temperature of a steel is estimated with the Andrews equation Ms(°C) = 539 − 423C − 30.4Mn − 17.7Ni − 12.1Cr − 7.5Mo (element symbols in mass%). Which is closest to the Ms temperature of a Cr–Mo steel with 0.40% C, 0.70% Mn, 1.0% Cr, 0.20% Mo and 0% Ni?
choices: About 335 °C
About 370 °C
About 504 °C
heat-treatment-025.explanation: The terms are 423 × 0.40 = 169.2, 30.4 × 0.70 ≈ 21.3, 12.1 × 1.0 = 12.1 and 7.5 × 0.20 = 1.5, so Ms ≈ 539 − 169.2 − 21.3 − 12.1 − 1.5 ≈ 335 °C. About 370 °C subtracts only the carbon term, and about 504 °C leaves out the carbon term. As the coefficients show, carbon lowers Ms most strongly, and every alloying element listed here also lowers it. The lower the Ms, the more retained austenite remains untransformed when the steel is quenched to room temperature. The equation is empirical, fitted to steels in a limited composition range, so for high-alloy steels it is only a rough guide.
